The Short AnswerChilies feel spicy because the chemical capsaicin tricks your tongue's heat-sensing TRPV1 receptors into signaling actual burning heat to the brain. The difference between true taste and chemesthesis The spicy heat delivered by chili peppers is not one of the five basic gustatory tastes; instead, it is a neurological pain and temperature sensation known as chemesthesis. True tastes like sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami are detected by specialized taste receptor cells organized in lingual taste buds. In contrast, the fiery sensation of a chili pepper is triggered by sensory nerve endings belonging to the trigeminal cranial nerve. Chemical education publications from the American Chemical Society demonstrate that pungency results from chemical activation of protective thermal and physical pain receptors rather than nutrient detection. The chemical compound responsible for this physiological reaction is capsaicin, along with a family of related chemical molecules termed capsaicinoids. Capsaicin is an odorless, hydrophobic alkaloid synthesized exclusively in plants of the genus Capsicum. When you bite into a hot pepper, capsaicin molecules rapidly dissolve into saliva and diffuse across the mucosal membranes lining your tongue, gums, and oral cavity. passages.text: Heat Is Not Flavour: What Chili Peppers Really Taste Like Ask any experienced cook whether the hottest pepper in the pantry is also the most flavourful — chances are the answer will be a firm no. Heat and flavour in chili peppers are not simply different in degree; they are different in kind, produced by entirely separate chemical mechanisms and perceived by entirely different parts of your nervous system. Why Heat Is Not a Taste When capsaicin — the primary pungent compound in chili peppers — reaches your mouth, it does not activate your taste buds. Instead, it binds to a receptor called TRPV1 (transient receptor potential vanilloid 1), a protein that normally responds to dangerously high temperatures above around 43 °C. Capsaicin essentially tricks this receptor into firing as though your mouth were being scalded, triggering a cascade of pain and heat signals that travel to the brain via sensory nerve fibres. This is a neurological alarm response, not a flavour signal. The gustatory system — the one responsible for sweetness, saltiness, bitterness, sourness, and umami — plays no role in perceiving heat.
